title: What the parties say on religion and state
question: Who should run marriage, conversion and Shabbat rules?
note: Shas and UTJ rows quote the Jerusalem Post's summary of the two parties' positions, and the Yashar row the Jewish Chronicle's; neither is the party's own text. Religious Zionism–Zehut and Noam rows come from israel2026.co.il, an aggregator site, not the parties' own pages. Likud and Otzma Yehudit rows describe their record in the 25th Knesset; no 2026 religion-and-state statement was found for either. No published position found for People of Israel, Reservists–Economic, Blue and White, the Joint List or Ra'am (checked October 2026); their rows give older or adjacent material, which sets no stance.

rows.text: Jerusalem Post summary of Shas and UTJ: "They have firmly opposed expanding alternatives to religious law, including civil marriage"; on conversion they "favor keeping the authority to do so within the Orthodox religious establishment"; they "oppose changes that would expand non-Orthodox forms of worship at the Western Wall." Shas championed the July 2026 law returning kosher certification to the Chief Rabbinate (Times of Israel).
Same positions as Shas in the Jerusalem Post summary. MK Moshe Gafni, sponsor of the Torah study Basic Law: "This Basic Law will serve as the state's moral compass."

Record: governed with Shas and UTJ as the kashrut, rabbinical-court and Torah study laws passed. On the Western Wall bill, Netanyahu let Likud and coalition MKs vote freely; Justice Minister Yariv Levin (Likud) backed it, saying it would "put an end to the High Court's interference in the management of the Western Wall."

Record: MK Limor Son Har-Melech sponsored the July 2026 law allowing gender-segregated master's and doctoral programs, to "advance women from sectors that have not received the opportunities they deserve."
"Jewish identity in education and state institutions."
"Preserving Shabbat in public space and strengthening the Orthodox rabbinate, conversion and kashrut." Its leader, Avi Maoz, sponsored the Western Wall bill.

The Jewish Chronicle's summary: "a secular party, but not anti-religious" that "supports civil marriage, divorce and same-sex marriage," with a "'live and let live' approach to Shabbat observance, devolving decisions to municipalities." Eisenkot (Jerusalem Post, Sep 24, 2026): "I am not religious, but I grew up in a traditional family and have profound respect for Judaism and tradition."

Lapid: "In the State of Israel, there should be a parallel civil marriage option for anyone who wants it," with legislation on equal rights for every couple sought within the first 100 days of the next government (Sep 15, 2026). Bennett, Apr 20, 2026, before the B'Yachad merger: "We should allow cities to choose whether they want public transportation on Shabbat."

"Promote civil marriage"; "promote the operation of public transport on Shabbat in a limited format in secular localities"; "extend recognition of conversion to other religious bodies in addition to the Chief Rabbinate."

"We will demand the implementation of civil marriage and divorce options within Israel"; "Tel Aviv will not impose Shabbat transportation on Bnei Brak, and Bnei Brak will not impose its way of life on Tel Aviv"; the Western Wall compromise as drafted by Avichai Mandelblit and Natan Sharansky.

No position found on marriage, conversion, Shabbat or the Rabbinate. The party's founding principles call for "a state where Judaism invites and does not coerce, includes and does not dictate" (translated).
rows.source: People of Israel, founding principles (Hebrew, undated)

rows.text: No 2026 position found. Its 2019 platform would "allow personal choice in marriage matters" and let local authorities that want it run transport on Shabbat (translated). In 2021 Gantz sought civil marriage registration, saying "many are having their basic right to marry taken away from them."
rows.source: Zman Yisrael, Sep 11, 2019; Times of Israel, Feb 15, 2021

rows.text: No position found for the list. Yoaz Hendel, as communications minister in 2021: "We must provide an alternative for those unable to marry" (translated).
No joint 2026 platform found. Hadash's platform, as quoted in 2019, calls for "separation of religion from state" and civil marriage and divorce (translated).

No position found on marriage, conversion or Shabbat. Mansour Abbas, on cutting the party's ties with its religious council: "Ra'am today is moving in the direction of being a completely civic party, with separate institutions."
